objective: Write, solve, and graph inequalities to plan a class Game Day.
instructions: Help Maya and Eli plan Game Day. Stay within the money and time limits. Solve each problem, explain your thinking, and finish the mastery check.
opening: Your class is planning Game Day: team games, snacks, and a short video from past students. Maya and Eli need your help to decide how many game rounds the class can play.

stages.title: Stay within the budget
stages.story: Your class has $90 for Game Day. Snacks cost $18 total. A small prize for each game round costs $6. How many rounds can you afford? Let x be the number of rounds.
teach: An inequality shows a limit. “At most $90” means you can spend $90 or less.
Use ≤ for “at most” and ≥ for “at least.” The line under the sign means “or equal to.”
Use < for “less than” and > for “more than.” These signs leave out the exact number.
For Game Day, write 18 + 6x ≤ 90. The 18 pays for snacks. The 6x pays for prizes.
Solve to find how many rounds fit the budget. Count whole rounds: no half rounds or negative rounds.
worked: At the carnival, entry is $8 and each ride ticket is $4. You have $44.
You can buy up to 9 tickets. Nine costs exactly $44; fewer tickets also fit the budget.

questions.prompt: Snacks cost $18, plus $6 for a prize each round. Which inequality keeps the total at $90 or less?
questions.hint: “At most” means less than OR equal to the limit.
questions.explanation: 18 + 6x ≤ 90 means the snack and prize costs stay at $90 or less.

questions.prompt: Game Day snacks cost $18. Prizes cost $6 per round. You have $90. Solve the inequality for x, the number of rounds.
questions.hint: Subtract 18 from both sides. Then divide both sides by positive 6; keep the inequality sign pointing the same way.
questions.explanation: Subtract 18: 6x ≤ 72. Divide by 6: x ≤ 12. You can afford up to 12 rounds.

questions.prompt: More than 8 students want to join Game Day. Let v be the number of students. Which answer matches?

choices.text: v > 8: the smallest possible number of students is 9.

questions.explanation: “More than 8” leaves out 8. The smallest whole number that works is 9.

stages.reflection: Explain why both 10 and 12 rounds fit the $90 budget.
stages.reveal: The first hidden clip shows students filming their empty lunch table, then filling it with friends who usually avoid the camera. A caption reads: “Save a place for someone new.” The archive is about belonging, not a secret prize.
stages.exampleIntro: Try a school carnival first. You have $44. Entry costs $8, and ride tickets cost $4 each. Let t be the number of tickets. Work through one step at a time.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 1 · The total cost is 8 + 4t. Which comparison means spend at most $44?
exampleSteps.hint: At most allows spending exactly $44 and spending less.
exampleSteps.explanation: Use ≤ to include the spending limit and every cheaper plan.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 2 · In 8 + 4t ≤ 44, how do we undo the $8 entry fee on both sides?

choices.text: Divide only the right side by 4

exampleSteps.hint: Undo addition with subtraction. Keep the comparison balanced.
exampleSteps.explanation: Subtracting the same amount preserves the inequality direction.

exampleSteps.hint: Pay the $8 entry fee first. How much of the $44 is left?
exampleSteps.explanation: 4t ≤ 36. Now the remaining budget is available for tickets.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 4 · Divide both sides of 4t ≤ 36 by positive 4. Complete t ≤ ___.
exampleSteps.hint: Compute 36 ÷ 4. Dividing by a positive number preserves ≤.
exampleSteps.explanation: t ≤ 9 means you can buy 9 tickets or fewer.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 5 · Nine tickets cost 8 + 4(9) = $44. Can you afford 9 tickets?

choices.text: Yes, and 9 is the only solution

exampleSteps.hint: The symbol ≤ includes equality. Also test a smaller number.
exampleSteps.explanation: Nine works. Eight works too because 8 + 4(8) = 40 ≤ 44.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 6 · Which ticket counts can you actually buy?

choices.text: Any whole number of tickets from 0 through 9
Negative tickets or part of a ticket, such as −2 or 8.5

exampleSteps.hint: Tickets are counted in whole numbers. You can buy fewer than the maximum.
exampleSteps.explanation: You can buy 0 through 9 whole tickets. You do not have to spend every dollar.

stages.title: Show answers on a number line
stages.story: A number line helps the class see which times work. Let t mean minutes. A game break must be at least 5 minutes. The opening video must be less than 9 minutes.
teach: Start at the number in the inequality. For t ≥ 5, start at 5.
Use a filled circle for ≤ or ≥: the number is allowed. Use an open circle for < or >: it is not allowed.
Shade left for smaller numbers. Shade right for larger numbers.
Example: t > 5 has an open circle at 5 and shading to the right. A time of 5.5 minutes works, but 5 minutes does not.
worked: Solve 3t + 2 < 20. Subtract 2, then divide by 3: t < 6.
Use an open circle at 6 because 6 is not allowed.
Shade left. For example, 5 works: 3(5) + 2 = 17, and 17 < 20.
If t counts game rounds, the whole rounds that work are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

questions.prompt: Graph x ≤ 12 on the number line.
questions.hint: Think about which numbers make x ≤ 12 true. Does 12 itself work? Are the other solutions smaller or larger?
questions.explanation: Fill the circle at 12 and shade left. Twelve and smaller numbers work.

questions.prompt: A game break lasts at least 5 minutes. Graph t ≥ 5.
questions.hint: Five is allowed. Times longer than 5 minutes are allowed too.
questions.explanation: Fill the circle at 5 and shade right. Five minutes and longer times work.

questions.prompt: The opening video must be less than 9 minutes. Graph t < 9.
questions.explanation: Use an open circle at 9 and shade left. Nine is not allowed; shorter times work.

stages.reflection: Choose one graph. Explain its circle and which way you shaded.
stages.reveal: A second clip shows a student saying: “I thought nobody would remember my drawing.” The rover projects the same tiny star logo Maya found on the receiver receipt. The anonymous broadcast was a collaboration across clubs.
stages.exampleIntro: Try this with less help: solve 3t + 2 < 20, then graph your answer. Use a hint if you need one.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 1 · Subtract 2 from both sides. Complete 3t < ___.
Step 2 · Solve this inequality for t.
exampleSteps.explanation: t < 6 means t must be less than 6. Six is not allowed.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 3 · Graph the solution of 3t + 2 < 20 on the number line.
exampleSteps.hint: Test t = 6 for the circle and t = 5 for the shading direction.
exampleSteps.explanation: Open circle at 6, shade left: 3(6) + 2 = 20 fails, while 3(5) + 2 = 17 works.

exampleSteps.prompt: Step 4 · If t counts game rounds, which whole numbers work?

choices.text: Negative rounds or parts of a round, such as −1 or 2.5

exampleSteps.hint: Use whole numbers below 6. Six is not allowed.
exampleSteps.explanation: The possible round counts are 0 through 5. Six does not work because the sign is <.

stages.title: Solve with a negative number
stages.story: Game Day lasts 50 minutes. Each round takes 4 minutes. The class needs at least 14 minutes left for cleanup. Eli writes 50 − 4x ≥ 14, but gets x ≥ 9. Would playing more rounds really leave more cleanup time?
teach: Divide both sides by −4. When you divide by a negative number, flip the sign: x ≤ 9.
Why flip? Negatives reverse order: 2 < 5, but −2 > −5.
Check the story: 9 rounds use 36 minutes, leaving 14 for cleanup. Ten rounds leave only 10 minutes. You can play at most 9 rounds.
worked: Another game has 40 minutes, takes 3 minutes per round, and needs more than 10 minutes left.
Divide by −3 and flip the sign: r < 10.
Nine rounds leave 13 minutes. Ten rounds leave exactly 10, which is not more than 10.

questions.prompt: You have 50 minutes. Each round takes 4 minutes. Keep at least 14 minutes for cleanup. Solve for x, the number of rounds.
questions.hint: After subtracting 50, divide by −4 and reverse the relation.
questions.explanation: −4x ≥ −36 gives x ≤ 9 after dividing by −4 and flipping the sign. Play 9 rounds or fewer.

questions.prompt: Eli got x ≥ 9. Why is that wrong?

choices.text: Dividing by −4 should flip ≥ to ≤. Ten rounds leave too little cleanup time.
Inequalities can never have negative coefficients.

questions.hint: Which step uses a negative multiplier or divisor? Then test 10.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a negative flips the sign. Ten rounds use 40 minutes and leave only 10, so x ≥ 9 cannot be right.

questions.prompt: Another class has 62 minutes. Each round takes 5 minutes. They need more than 17 minutes for cleanup. Solve for x.
questions.explanation: Subtract 62: −5x > −45. Divide by −5 and flip: x < 9. Nine rounds leave exactly 17 minutes, so 9 is not allowed.

stages.reflection: Show why 9 rounds leave enough cleanup time but 10 rounds do not.
stages.reveal: The next fragment is a recording of an ordinary school bell followed by laughter. “We almost deleted this because it wasn’t impressive,” a voice says. “Keep it. Ordinary days become history too.” Only the final combined schedule remains locked.

stages.title: Choose a plan that works
stages.story: The class wants at least 6 rounds. The $90 snack-and-prize budget allows up to 12. The time limit allows up to 9. Choose a number that works for all three rules.
teach: Check all three rules: at least 6 rounds, no more than 12 for the budget, and no more than 9 for time.
The whole numbers that work are 6, 7, 8, and 9.
To play the most rounds, choose 9. It costs $72 and leaves 14 minutes for cleanup.
To spend the least money, choose 6. It costs $54 and leaves 26 minutes for cleanup.
worked: Another class wants at least 4 rounds. Money allows up to 10, but time allows fewer than 8.
The possible whole counts are 4, 5, 6, and 7.
Choose 7 to play the most rounds. Eight is not allowed.
Choose 4 to spend the least if each round costs money.

questions.prompt: The rules are x ≥ 6, x ≤ 12, and x ≤ 9. Which list shows every whole number of rounds that works?
What is the greatest number of rounds you can play and still meet all three rules?
questions.hint: Choose the largest number that meets every rule.
questions.explanation: Nine rounds meet every rule. Ten would leave too little cleanup time.

questions.prompt: The class wants to spend the least money while meeting every rule. Which plan should it choose?

choices.text: 6 rounds: $54 total and 26 minutes left for cleanup.
9 rounds: more rounds must cost less.
0 rounds: ignore the rule that asks for at least 6.

questions.explanation: Six is the smallest number that meets every rule. Each extra round adds $6.

stages.reflection: Choose 6 or 9 rounds. Explain why you chose it, what it costs, and how much cleanup time is left.
stages.reveal: All fragments join. The old crew’s final message appears: “Don’t just watch our year. Add yours.” The archive includes an empty slot labeled NEXT CREW. The tiny star is not a code to a prize—it is an invitation to leave one honest piece of school life for the students who follow you.

forms.prompt: Another class has $65. Snacks cost $15, and prizes cost $5 per round. Solve for x, the number of rounds.
forms.explanation: The answer is x ≤ 10. 5x ≤ 50 gives x ≤ 10; equality is allowed.

forms.prompt: Graph t > 4 on the number line.
forms.explanation: The answer is t > 4. Open circle at 4; shade right. 4 is not a solution.

forms.prompt: You have 48 minutes. Each round takes 6 minutes. Keep at least 12 minutes for cleanup. Solve for x, the number of rounds.
forms.explanation: The answer is x ≤ 6. −6x ≥ −36 becomes x ≤ 6 after dividing by −6.

forms.prompt: The rules are x ≥ 4, x ≤ 10, and x ≤ 6. What is the greatest whole number of rounds that works?
forms.explanation: The common whole-number choices are 4, 5, 6. Maximum: 6.

forms.prompt: A planner claims the whole-number solutions of 3 ≤ x < 7 are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. What is the correction?

choices.text: Keep only 7, because it is the number shown after the inequality sign.

forms.prompt: Another class has $68. Snacks cost $20, and prizes cost $4 per round. Solve for x, the number of rounds.
forms.explanation: The answer is x ≤ 12. 4x ≤ 48 gives x ≤ 12. Twelve is included.

forms.prompt: Graph t ≥ 7 on the number line.
forms.explanation: The answer is t ≥ 7. Filled circle at 7; shade right. 7 is a solution.

forms.prompt: You have 55 minutes. Each round takes 5 minutes. Keep more than 15 minutes for cleanup. Solve for x, the number of rounds.
forms.explanation: The answer is x < 8. −5x > −40 gives x < 8 after dividing by −5. Eight is excluded.

forms.prompt: The rules are x ≥ 5, x ≤ 12, and x < 8. What is the greatest whole number of rounds that works?
forms.explanation: The whole numbers that work are 5, 6, and 7. Eight is not allowed because x < 8.

forms.prompt: You can play 5, 6, or 7 rounds. Each round costs the same amount. Which choice costs the least?

choices.text: 5 rounds, because it is the smallest allowed number.
7 rounds, because more rounds always cost less.
0 rounds, even though the class needs at least 5.

forms.explanation: Choose 5 rounds. It meets the rules and costs less than 6 or 7 rounds.

ending: Game Day is planned! The class has enough money for snacks and prizes, time for games, and time to clean up. Maya plays the old student video. Its message is simple: make room for everyone and leave something good for the next class.
reportPrompt: Choose a Game Day plan. Explain how many rounds you recommend, what they cost, and how much cleanup time is left.
